script: My robot baby exploded on the bus—watch the chaos that followed.. I was in 11th grade when our teacher handed us the "realcare baby," a robotic infant that cries nonstop. It needed a tamper‑proof wristband to be cared for, and the teacher would download a report on our parenting skills at the end. She said pick it up before school so you could troubleshoot, but I chose Friday afternoon to avoid being a mom during math. I had no rides, so I lugged the car seat onto a packed bus. People stared—half thinking I was a mom, half wondering why a 16‑year‑old had a realistic baby doll. About halfway to the station, the doll started whimpering. I pressed my ID bracelet to its chest. No chime. I tried again. Still no chime. The crying escalated. I slapped its chest, flipped it over, hit the neck and butt sensors. Nothing. Passengers looked confused. An older guy from the nearby care home offered parenting tips like it was a real baby, but the doll was a busted machine. I got off the bus. The crying was off the charts—like a baby on fire. I had two minutes to tap the ID or it would "neglect" and lose its mind. I was on the floor of the bus station, ripping off its pants to change its diaper, pressing the bottle to its face, rocking it with my knee, but it didn't care. Everyone heard the pure agony. Some asked if I was okay; most just sidestepped. I reached for my phone, only to find my backpack gone—forgot it on the bus. No phone, no wallet, no keys. I was stuck with an inconsolable robot baby. I bumped into a girl from school with her boyfriend. She let me email my teacher on her phone while she scoured the area for my bag. The teacher replied that she couldn't remotely shut it off and told me to hurry back before she left. I had to fix the backpack problem first. The boyfriend tried to joke, but the doll's neck snapped back and forth, then let out a scream that sounded like a dying animal. I felt like I'd triggered shaken baby syndrome. I and the doll sobbed together as I headed to the help desk, trying to remember the bus number. The employee was too exhausted to care. I waited an hour for the bus to return. The doll took short crying breaks, but I could still hear it when it stopped. I asked a woman if she'd call my dad and hold the phone up. She said no and backed away. I realized the teenage girl with mascara and a distressed doll was probably a scam. I didn't ask anyone else. Eventually the bus came back with my bag. I sprinted to grab it, leaving the doll in the car seat covered with a blanket by a station entrance. People gathered, eyes wide, asking if someone'd abandoned their baby. I lifted the blanket and explained the situation again. My phone was dead. I just wanted to go home. I couldn't check if my teacher was still at school and didn't think leaving it outside her classroom for someone to find at night was a good idea. I made it to the subway. People on the stairs smiled at me and my doll. A woman with a rough look approached and asked, "Your school lets you bring your baby?" I was not in the mood, but I explained and vented about the bullshit afternoon. She started an incoherent lecture about never letting a man talk you into unprotected sex. I nodded and rushed to a different car. I hid in a corner, covered the doll with the blanket, and tried to muffle the speaker with my hands. I prayed nobody would see me and think I was suffocating a real infant. I finally got home. I fought tears to explain what happened to my dad. He thought the doll was fine, maybe it just cried itself out. "Maybe we can just muffle it under some pillows in the basement." The doll's screaming for neglect grew louder. I felt maternal shame, even though it was a robot. I yelled, "I am sorry! I am trying to help you! It just won't let me!" My mom echoed my feelings. My teacher and I emailed back and forth. She eventually said we could bring it back to school, and a custodian would lock it in a classroom over the weekend. After 12 hours of neglect, it would automatically shut off. On the way there, my dad made a joke about the premium "colic baby" experience. We handed the doll to the sweet custodian, who locked it in a classroom to die.
